title: WMA Declaration of Helsinki – Ethical Principles for Medical Research Involving Human Participants (2024 revision)
publisher: World Medical Association; also published in JAMA 333(1):71 (2025)
edition_version: Adopted by the 75th WMA General Assembly, Helsinki, October 2024
key_findings: Para 23: the protocol must be reviewed and approved by an independent, transparent research ethics committee (with at least one lay member) before the research starts; amendments also need approval.

Paras 19-20: vulnerability can be fixed or situational; harms of excluding vulnerable groups must be weighed against harms of including them, and they may be included only if research responds to their needs and cannot be done in a less vulnerable group.
Paras 28-29: for people who cannot consent, a legally authorised representative decides; where the person can assent, assent must be sought in addition, and dissent should be respected.
The 2024 text uses 'participants' throughout.
athar_applications: Baseline principle for any ATHAR study framed as research: prior ethics-committee approval, assent plus guardian permission, and respect for a teen's 'no'.
Supports designing pilots so that a less vulnerable group (18-24 adults, teachers) is used first for anything not specific to 13-17.
limitations: Addresses medical research; applies to educational/game research only by analogy and through institutional policies that adopt it.
Does not mention children by name; age rules come from national law.

title: International Ethical Guidelines for Health-related Research Involving Humans (Guideline 17: research involving children and adolescents; Guideline 13: reimbursement and compensation)
authors: Council for International Organizations of Medical Sciences (CIOMS)
key_findings: Guideline 17: before research with children/adolescents, a parent or legally authorised representative must give permission AND the child's assent must be obtained in line with capacity, after age-tailored information; a child's refusal must generally be respected.

Guideline 17: for procedures without potential individual benefit, risks must be minimised and no more than minimal; an ethics committee may allow only a minor increase above minimal risk when social value is compelling and adults cannot be studied instead.

Guideline 13: participants should be reimbursed for expenses and compensated for time; compensation must not be large enough to be an undue inducement, should not scale with risk, and must be approved by a local ethics committee; guardians of non-consenting participants get only reimbursement.
athar_applications: Defines the 'minimal risk + no direct individual benefit' frame that best fits ATHAR's playtests; any design adding risk (e.g., stressful content, recording faces) must be justified or removed.
Incentive rule for pilots: small, time-based, given to the teen (e.g., book voucher), not scaled to effort, approved by the committee; parents get travel reimbursement only.
limitations: Health-related research scope; educational/UX use is by analogy.
Text read from a full-text copy hosted by a university (ihmt.unl.pt); CIOMS page itself only confirmed publication.

title: Ethical Research Involving Children (ERIC compendium)
publisher: UNICEF Office of Research – Innocenti, Florence
key_findings: International compendium (ERIC project, UNICEF Innocenti with Southern Cross University's Centre for Children and Young People and partners) aimed at upholding children's dignity, rights and wellbeing in all research regardless of setting.
Promotes a reflexive approach – critical thinking and ethical decision-making across disciplines, methods and countries – rather than a checklist; available in several languages via childethics.com.
Organises guidance around harms and benefits, informed consent, privacy and confidentiality, and payment and compensation (per project description).
athar_applications: Use as the default ethics reference for a non-medical teen study where national rules are silent (Lebanon, Kuwait, Egypt education research).
Reflexive questions can be adapted into ATHAR's pre-session checklist.
limitations: Compendium text itself not read in this session (childethics.com unreachable through proxy); content summarised from the catalogue record and project page.
Not available in Arabic per the catalogue record (French, Spanish, Korean, Turkish, Bahasa listed).

title: Ethical Guidelines for Educational Research, fifth edition (2024)
license: CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 (commercial use requires BERA permission)
key_findings: Para 11: researchers should consider approaching gatekeepers (schools) first and adopting the institution's own ethical approval and safeguarding procedures, which is usually a requirement; translation effects matter when working across languages.

Paras 23-26: consent principles apply to children as assent; best interests of the child are primary (UNCRC); materials must suit age and reading ability; opt-in consent preferred, opt-out acceptable only in some circumstances after checking local law.
Paras 29-30: sponsorship must be disclosed to participants; researchers should avoid work where commercial gain might compromise validity and must declare conflicts of interest.
Para 31: right to withdraw for any or no reason; no coercion or extra incentives to re-engage. Para 33: incentives must not impinge on free decision and must be reported.
Para 48: information sheets must state when confidentiality may be broken (e.g., abuse disclosures), and researchers should inform participants of a disclosure where safe.
athar_applications: Core template for ATHAR's school permission letter (gatekeeper first, school's safeguarding procedure adopted) and for the limits-of-confidentiality clause in assent/consent forms.
Because ATHAR is the product owner, BERA paras 29-30 require disclosing commercial sponsorship and favour an independent analyst for any claim-bearing study.
limitations: UK professional guidance, not law in Arab countries.
NC-ND licence: may be cited and paraphrased, not adapted commercially.

title: ICC/ESOMAR International Code on Market, Opinion and Social Research and Data Analytics (2025 revision)
key_findings: Defines 'child' as 12 and under and 'young person' as 13-17, unless applicable law defines otherwise.

Article 2: consent from a parent, legal guardian or responsible adult whenever children are data subjects and whenever the law requires it; researchers must determine age before collecting further personal data; special care for young people, appropriate to age and maturity.

Article 6(e) and definitions: any 'non-research activity' (promotional, commercial, customer-experience follow-up aimed at changing an individual's attitudes or actions) must be disclosed in advance, needs separate consent, and must be clearly separated from research.
Article 3: data minimisation – collect only what is reasonable and directly relevant to the research purpose.
athar_applications: Governs ATHAR's product/market tests that fall outside 'research': age check first, guardian consent for under-18 per Arab law, no mixing of playtest with marketing or sales (e.g., no school price pitch inside a student session).
Supports separating Experiment 3's commercial offer (to the school administration) from any data collection with students.
limitations: Self-regulatory code binding on ESOMAR members and adopting associations, not law.
Its under-13 'child' threshold is looser than Arab legal capacity ages (18-21); national law prevails as the Code itself states.

title: ESOMAR/GRBN Guideline on Research and Data Analytics with Children, Young People, and Other Vulnerable Individuals
license: Copy/distribute permitted with attribution and notice '© 2018 ESOMAR and GRBN' (no derivatives stated)
key_findings: Consent of the responsible adult and of the child is required before collecting personal data from any child; even after adult consent, the child's own consent must be obtained.
In a protected environment such as a school, the consent of those who manage the location is needed first, then of the responsible adults, before any child is approached.

Researchers must ask age before any other personal data; responsible-adult consent is also required for photographing or recording children – without it images and voices must be made unidentifiable or deleted.
Default ages where national law is silent: child 12 and under, young person 13-17; national law and cultural norms prevail.
athar_applications: Even a non-research 'product test' in a school needs the same chain: school management -> parent -> teen. ATHAR adopts this chain for every session type.
Recording rule maps to ATHAR's 'audio only, transcribe then delete' policy.
limitations: Market-research industry guidance; a 1999/2009 predecessor ('Interviewing Children and Young People') used under-14 as 'child' – superseded.

title: 45 CFR Part 46 (Common Rule) – §46.102 definitions of research, human subject and minimal risk; Subpart D additional protections for children (§§46.401-46.409)
authors: U.S. Department of Health and Human Services
edition_version: 2018 Requirements; eCFR text current as of 22-23 Oct 2026
key_findings: §46.102(l): research is a systematic investigation, including development, testing and evaluation, designed to develop or contribute to generalizable knowledge; §46.102(j): minimal risk = harm not greater than ordinarily encountered in daily life or routine tests.
§46.402: assent is a child's affirmative agreement; mere failure to object is not assent.
§46.408: one parent's permission suffices for minimal-risk research (§46.404); assent required when children are capable, judged by age, maturity and psychological state.

§46.401(c): for children, the survey/interview exemption (d)(2)(iii) and (d)(3) do not apply; (d)(2) applies only to educational tests and observation of public behaviour without investigator participation.
athar_applications: Supplies the operational test used in ATHAR's 'research vs product test' decision table: is the activity designed to produce generalizable knowledge (publishable claims, validity evidence)? If yes -> ethics review.
Even in US terms, interviews/surveys with minors are not exempt – ATHAR's think-aloud with 13-17 should be treated as at least expedited-review research when done for publication.
limitations: US federal rule; binding only on US-funded or US-institution research (e.g., AUB's FWA) – used here as a reference definition, not as Arab law.

title: The Belmont Report: Ethical Principles and Guidelines for the Protection of Human Subjects of Research (Part A: Boundaries between practice and research)
authors: National Commission for the Protection of Human Subjects of Biomedical and Behavioral Research
publisher: U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (OHRP)
key_findings: Practice = activities designed solely to benefit an individual with reasonable expectation of success; research = activity designed to test a hypothesis and contribute to generalizable knowledge, usually under a formal protocol.
A new or untested procedure is not research by that fact alone, but radically new procedures should be made the object of formal research early.
If an activity contains any element of research, it should undergo review for the protection of human subjects.
athar_applications: Underpins ATHAR's mixed-activity rule: a school pilot that both delivers lessons (practice) and collects validity evidence (research) is reviewed as research.
AUB IRB states it is guided by Belmont principles for all human-subjects research.
limitations: Biomedical/behavioural framing from 1979; still the reference text for Common Rule-based IRBs.

title: Quality Improvement Activities FAQs
authors: Office for Human Research Protections (OHRP), U.S. HHS
publisher: U.S. Department of Health and Human Services
key_findings: Quality-improvement work that only implements a practice and collects data for practical/administrative purposes is generally not research under 45 CFR 46.
Intent to publish does not by itself decide the question: non-research QI may be published, and a QI project can be research even with no plan to publish.
A project that introduces an untested intervention and collects outcome data to establish scientific evidence of its effect may be nonexempt human-subjects research.
athar_applications: Directly governs ATHAR's decision table: a usability/fun playtest feeding product decisions can be non-research; an A/B test designed to show the argument screen 'works' (Experiment 2) is research.
Warns against relabelling: calling Experiment 2 'product optimisation' does not remove the research character if its purpose is generalizable evidence.
limitations: Non-binding guidance; predates 2018 Requirements; publication date not shown on page.

title: Implementing Regulations of the Law of Ethics of Research on Living Creatures (NCBE) – English translation (Second Edition, Second Revised version, 1437H/2016)
title_ar: اللائحة التنفيذية لنظام أخلاقيات البحث على المخلوقات الحية
authors: National Committee of BioEthics (NCBE), King Abdulaziz City for Science and Technology
publisher: NCBE / KACST; translation hosted by King Saud University (dsrs.ksu.edu.sa)
edition_version: 2nd edition, 2nd revised version (1437H-2016); a 3rd edition dated 25/9/1443H (2022) exists per qanoniah.com – not read
key_findings: Art. 25.1: research on minors requires informed consent from parents or legal guardian, who must be told the level/probability of risk 'as well as the person's assent'; either parent may consent; either may withdraw at any phase.

Art. 25.2: the local committee approves research on minors only if it cannot be done on competent persons, the minor's interest requires it and risk is no more than minimal, the protocol minimises risk, and risk/benefit is documented; Art. 25.5: the committee may require an independent lawyer to represent the minor's interest.

Art. 10.18: expedited review (by chair or delegate) is available when risk does not exceed minimal and the research does not reveal identity; it also lists audio/video recording of behaviour without violating privacy. Art. 10.20: amendments to interviews/surveys with any 'vulnerable groups' (defined in Art. 1 to include those lacking legal capacity, i.e. minors) stay with the full committee, not the chair. [Corrected/Clarified 2026-10-27 by deep-card review]

Art. 10.32: the committee may exempt from periodic follow-up research involving educational tests, surveys, interviews or observation unless identities are recorded or participation could expose someone to liability; and research conducted for educational purposes.
Art. 10.24: recruitment advertisements must be approved by the local committee in advance.
athar_applications: Gives ATHAR's Saudi path: minimal-risk, de-identified playtests qualify for expedited review; identity-revealing recordings push toward full review – a strong reason for audio-only, transcribe-and-delete.
Flyers or WhatsApp recruitment messages to parents must be committee-approved before use (Art. 10.24).
Art. 25.2(1) 'cannot be done on competent persons' – ATHAR must justify why 13-17 (not 18-24) are needed: the product targets them and reading/fun responses differ by age.
limitations: 2016 edition; the current 3rd edition (2022) was identified (qanoniah.com) but its text was behind login and the KAUST copy returned 404 – article numbers may have changed.

English translation; the Arabic text prevails. No 'Draft of Translation' marking was found in the downloaded PDF (text layer and page images checked). [Corrected/Clarified 2026-10-27 by deep-card review]

title: The Saudi Law of Ethics of Research on Living Creatures and its Implementing Regulations
key_findings: Saudi Arabia passed the Law and Implementing Regulations on 14/09/1431H (24/08/2010).
The system combines Islamic Shariah with international research ethics guidelines and, per the author, contains all core ethical requirements for research.
Author proposes it as a model for other Arab and Islamic countries (abstract).
athar_applications: Secondary confirmation of the 2010 law date and its Shariah-plus-international structure; useful when explaining to Saudi partners why ATHAR's protocol cites both CIOMS and the national law.
limitations: Abstract only read (PubMed); first published online 2016, issue 2017.
Medical focus; does not settle application to educational research.

title: Facilitating a researcher's mission (تسهيل مهمة باحث أو باحثة) – Unaizah Education Department e-service
title_ar: تسهيل مهمة باحث أو باحثة — إدارة التعليم بمحافظة عنيزة
authors: Ministry of Education, Saudi Arabia – Unaizah Education Department
key_findings: Eligible applicants: university and graduate students inside or outside the Kingdom, and researchers from government, private and non-profit sectors; request must come officially from the applicant's university/affiliated body via the 'Aamali' correspondence system.

The department (Development and Transformation Dept – Institutional Performance Measurement Division) reviews the request and the research instruments, may require changes, and issues a facilitation letter for the target sample; stated duration 3 working days.

Conditions: submit well before exams and holidays; instruments must fit national values; confidentiality; no sensitive data without approval; parental consent where the study needs it; deliver a copy of the completed study.
athar_applications: Saudi school access for Experiments 1 and 3 runs through the regional Education Department's facilitation letter, requested by the partner university (not by ATHAR as a company).
Instruments (think-aloud prompts, surveys) must be submitted for review – keep them short, neutral and value-compatible.
limitations: One regional department's page; other regions (e.g., Riyadh) may differ in unit name and timing. Ethics-committee approval is not listed as a required document here – but the university side normally requires it.

title: Personal Data Protection Law (Saudi Arabia) – Art. 27 (processing for scientific, research or statistical purposes without consent) and Art. 28
publisher: SDAIA National Data Governance Platform – Knowledge Center
key_findings: Art. 27: personal data may be collected/processed for scientific, research or statistical purposes without consent only if (1) the data do not specifically identify the person, (2) identifiers will be destroyed during processing before disclosure and the data are not sensitive, or (3) another law or a prior agreement with the person requires it; the Regulations set controls.
Art. 28: official identity documents may not be photographed or copied except where law requires or a competent public entity requests.
athar_applications: Even with the research exception, ATHAR still needs guardian consent because pilots involve identifiable minors in live sessions – the exception only helps for later analysis of de-identified logs.
Never photograph student IDs or national IDs to verify age/guardianship in pilots (Art. 28).
limitations: Same law already catalogued as ATH-SRC-1049 (general record); this record isolates the research articles. Merge step may fold it into ATH-SRC-1049.

title: Educational research requests in government schools: Ministry of Education completes them within 6 weeks (التربية: 6 أسابيع لإنجاز طلبات البحوث التربوية)
title_ar: التربية: 6 أسابيع لإنجاز طلبات البحوث التربوية
key_findings: The UAE Ministry of Education opened a service for applications to conduct educational research in government schools (also for publishing results and conferences).
Target applicants: master's and PhD students, university faculty and research teams, and educational/research institutions; others are assessed case by case.
Processing up to 6 weeks, free; required: proof of ethics approval from the applicant's university or research institution, and copies of data-collection instruments.
athar_applications: For UAE government schools ATHAR must partner with a university or research institution that holds the ethics approval; budget ≥6 weeks for MoE processing.
Private schools are regulated by emirate authorities (KHDA Dubai, ADEK Abu Dhabi, RAK DOK) – separate path.
limitations: Press report; official MoE service page not reached. Does not mention parental consent or data rules.

title: Approval Process for External Research in Ras Al Khaimah Private Schools (RAKDOK-POL-2025-15, v01)
authors: Ras Al Khaimah Department of Knowledge (RAK DOK)
edition_version: Version 01, effective 1 July 2025 (issue date also shown as 1 Aug 2025)
key_findings: External researchers submit a proposal (objectives, methods, participant ages/grades, instruments attached, analysis, ethical considerations, timeline, dissemination) to RAK DOK's External Research Review Committee.

After approval RAK DOK facilitates contact; the researcher must obtain school board and parent approvals and informed consent of students as appropriate; the principal makes the final decision; approval does not guarantee access.

Collect only strictly necessary data; anonymise and store securely per UAE law; no third-party sharing without explicit written consent of RAK DOK and stakeholders; researchers are 'encouraged' (not required) to share findings with RAK DOK and schools before publication, and RAK DOK reserves the right not to approve publication; researchers must also obtain 'all necessary security clearances' (s.2.4). [Corrected/Clarified 2026-10-27 by deep-card review]
athar_applications: Template for what any UAE emirate regulator will ask: full instrument copies, data-minimisation plan, dissemination plan; ATHAR's protocol pack should be built to this standard once and reused.
Pre-publication review by the regulator must be negotiated before Experiment 1's 'publishable response-process report' is promised.
limitations: RAK private schools only; Dubai (KHDA) and Abu Dhabi (ADEK) equivalents not found online in this session. No review turnaround stated.

The PDF footer states the policy is to be treated as confidential and not copied without RAK DOK's written permission; do not store it in 99_LEGAL_SOURCE_ASSETS - link only. [Corrected/Clarified 2026-10-27 by deep-card review]

title: DSREC Documentation Procedure for Student Research (Dubai Scientific Research Ethics Committee) – submission checklist
authors: Dubai Health Authority – Medical Education & Research Department, Medical Research Section
key_findings: DSREC student submissions require an application form, study proposal, participant information sheet and consent form written in both Arabic and English, data-collection tools, questionnaires in English and Arabic, a confidentiality agreement and proof of enrolment.
Eligibility is tied to universities recognised by the UAE Ministry of Higher Education or KHDA.
athar_applications: Confirms the UAE norm of bilingual (Arabic+English) consent and instruments – ATHAR templates are drafted bilingual accordingly.
DSREC is a health-sector committee; it is not the route for a non-health educational playtest, but shows what Dubai ethics reviewers expect.
limitations: Health-research committee; scope for educational/game research not established.

title: Monitoring and Compliance and certifying IRB/HREC – National Center for Health Research (MOHAP)
authors: Ministry of Health and Prevention (MOHAP), UAE – National Center for Health Research
key_findings: MOHAP, through the National Center for Health Research, is introducing a certification scheme requiring HRECs/IRBs to follow National Guidelines to protect participants in clinical trials and health research.
The page addresses health research only; no mention of social, behavioural or educational research or of minors.
athar_applications: Indicates the UAE federal ethics-committee framework is health-oriented; ATHAR's non-health study should rely on a university research ethics committee plus education-authority permission.
limitations: No legal basis, document title or date on the page.

title: Law No. 214 of 2020 Promulgating the Law to Regulate Clinical Medical Research (Egypt) – English translation (Official Gazette Issue 51 bis (F), 23 Dec 2020)
title_ar: القانون رقم 214 لسنة 2020 بإصدار قانون تنظيم البحوث الطبية الإكلينيكية
key_findings: Promulgation Art. 1: the law applies to clinical medical research conducted on humans and their medical data at research entities in Egypt.

Art. 1 defines 'clinical research' around therapeutic, preventive, diagnostic and similar interventions; 'research intervention' may include non-invasive methods such as health surveys, education and questionnaires (within clinical medical studies).

Art. 3: research on vulnerable groups only if necessary and related to a condition affecting them, with consent of parents/guardian; Art. 4: protocol approved by the competent institutional review board.
athar_applications: An educational game playtest is not 'clinical medical research' – this law is not ATHAR's route in Egypt; the relevant gates are the Ministry of Education/school, a university REC if academic, and Law 151/2020 for children's data (ATH-SRC-1061).
Avoid health-like measures (stress scales, wellbeing screening) in Egyptian pilots so the study cannot be construed as health research.
limitations: English translation on the regulator's site; Arabic Gazette text prevails. Executive regulation (PM Decree 927/2022) identified but not read.

title: Presidential Decree-Law No. 2915 of 1964 establishing the Central Agency for Public Mobilization and Statistics (CAPMAS) – text as published, incl. Art. 10 on publication of statistics
title_ar: القانون رقم 2915 لسنة 1964 بإنشاء وتنظيم الجهاز المركزي للتعبئة العامة والإحصاء
publisher: Parlmany (Al-Youm Al-Sabea parliamentary portal) – reproduction, 12 Jan 2016
key_findings: Art. 10 bars any ministry, authority, entity or individual (public or private) from publishing statistical results/data not produced by CAPMAS without the agency's approval.
Art. 6 empowers CAPMAS to decide which statistics and censuses the state needs and who carries them out.
athar_applications: Publishing survey-type statistics from Egyptian teen pilots may need CAPMAS approval; field practice (reported widely, not verified here) is to obtain CAPMAS approval for questionnaires before fieldwork – confirm with Egyptian counsel before Experiment 1 in Egypt.
Favour qualitative think-aloud reporting over population-style statistics for Egyptian pilots until clarified.
limitations: Secondary reproduction on a news portal, not the Official Gazette; the implementing decisions on prior questionnaire approval were not located in this session.

title: AUB Institutional Review Board – About us (Human Research Protection Program; Biomedical and Social & Behavioral Sciences review)
authors: American University of Beirut – Human Research Protection Program
key_findings: AUB's IRB reviews all human-subjects research by AUB/AUBMC faculty, students and staff regardless of funding or location, with Biomedical and Social & Behavioral Sciences (behavioural, educational, survey) streams.
Risk-tiered review: less than minimal risk -> exempt (granted only after IRB review of the submission), minimal risk -> expedited, more than minimal -> full board.
AUB holds a US Federal-wide Assurance (FWA) and applies Belmont principles to all research; an SBS consent template (2026) is published.
athar_applications: Lebanese path for Experiments 1-2: partner with an AUB (or LAU/USJ/LU) faculty member as PI so the study goes through an SBS IRB; ATHAR staff act as co-investigators.
Expect 'expedited' categorisation for de-identified, minimal-risk playtests with minors – exemption is unlikely because surveys/interviews with minors are not exempt under the US rule AUB follows.
limitations: Scope limited to AUB-affiliated researchers; external companies cannot apply directly (not confirmed on page). FWA number not shown.

title: USJ University Ethics Centre / Research Ethics Committee (CER) – letter template: approval to conduct research inside an educational institution
title_ar: جامعة القديس يوسف — المركز الجامعي للأخلاقيات، لجنة أخلاقيات البحث: الموافقة على إجراء بحث داخل المؤسسة
authors: Université Saint-Joseph de Beyrouth – Centre Universitaire d'Éthique
key_findings: Template letter from a USJ researcher to the head of an educational institution requesting permission to conduct research there, stating the project was approved by USJ's ethics council.

It lists the requested activities (individual interviews, group sessions, online questionnaire), states participation is voluntary, that interviews will be recorded for analysis, data used only for the research and kept confidential, and participants not identified.
Ends with a signed consent block for the institution's director.
athar_applications: Shows Lebanese practice: the school head's written consent is obtained after university ethics approval; ATHAR's school permission template mirrors this structure in Arabic.
Recording is disclosed up-front to the school; ATHAR goes further by limiting to audio and deleting after transcription.
limitations: University template, not a ministry rule; does not cover public-school ministry permission.

title: HDF Ethics Committee (Hôtel-Dieu de France / USJ) – legal basis of ethics committees in Lebanon
authors: Université Saint-Joseph – Hôtel-Dieu de France Ethics Committee
key_findings: Cites Lebanese Law 288/1994 (Code of Medical Ethics), Law 574/2004 on patients' rights and informed consent (Art. 11 requires an ethics committee in each hospital for clinical research), and Ministry of Public Health Decision 1/141 of 27 Jan 2016 creating an accreditation mechanism for ethics committees approving clinical trials and human-subject research.
The accreditation concerns biomedical/clinical research; social or educational research is not addressed.
athar_applications: Confirms that Lebanon's statutory ethics-committee framework is health-sector; for an educational game study ATHAR relies on a university SBS IRB (not on the MoPH system).
limitations: Secondary description by one committee; the MoPH decision text itself was not read.

title: Clinical research ethics review process in Lebanon: efficiency and functions of research ethics committees – results from a descriptive questionnaire-based study
key_findings: Surveyed university-hospital RECs in Lebanon on adherence to the national 'Standards and Operational Guidance for Ethics Review of Health-related Research with Human Participants'.
Confirms Lebanon's REC system is organised around health-related research in university hospitals.
athar_applications: Background for Lebanon: the mature REC infrastructure sits in university hospitals; ATHAR should seek an education/psychology faculty REC rather than a hospital REC.
limitations: Abstract-level reading; clinical-trial focus.

title: Handbook for Ethical Rules and Regulations for Research Involving Human Subjects (Qatar University, Office of Research)
authors: Qatar University – Office of Academic Research
key_findings: States IRB requirements comply with the Qatari Supreme Council of Health (now MoPH) requirements and apply to social as well as natural sciences.

§2.2.2: exempt categories (registered and approved by the research office) include normal educational practices in established educational settings and educational tests/surveys/interviews/observation – but exemption (b) cannot be used for minors for surveys, interviews or observation.

§2.2.1: expedited review covers research on individual/group characteristics or behaviour (cognition, language, social behaviour, surveys, interviews) and recordings made for research; the chair cannot approve changes to interviews/surveys with children alone.

§2.5: parental permission required; assent should be obtained and documented for children capable of it (age bands given, with internal inconsistencies between 12+, 13-14 and 14+); assent witness should be outside the family and the study.
athar_applications: Qatar path: QU (or another MoPH-registered IRB) expedited review for think-aloud/interviews with 13-17; plan a neutral assent witness (e.g., school counsellor not involved in ATHAR).
Classroom delivery of ATHAR cases as normal instruction could fit the 'normal educational practice' exemption, but any interview or survey of minors pushes the study back to expedited review.
limitations: Undated handbook referencing 2000-2007 documents and the former Supreme Council of Health; the current MoPH 'Policies, Regulations and Guidelines for Research Involving Human Subjects' could not be fetched (access denied).
Assent age bands are internally inconsistent in the handbook.

title: QU-IRB – Qatar University Institutional Review Board (requirements page)
authors: Qatar University – Research Planning & Development, Research Excellence
key_findings: Any research involving human subjects must undergo IRB review; QU-IRB ensures proposals comply with MoPH regulations and directives.
Assent forms are mandatory for children aged 7 to 17.
Researchers complete social-behavioural-educational ethics training (CITI SBS course in English or an Arabic SBS ethics video).
athar_applications: Qatar requires documented assent from every 13-17 participant – ATHAR assent template must be signed/recorded, not just verbal.
ATHAR moderators should complete SBS ethics training (CITI SBS or equivalent) before running sessions – a low-cost credibility step in all markets.
limitations: Does not mention MoEHE school permission; MoPH policy document not reachable.

title: Challenges to obtaining parental permission for child participation in a school-based waterpipe tobacco smoking prevention intervention in Qatar
key_findings: In 40 randomly selected Doha schools (grades 7-8), 53% of parents (2308/4314) returned permission forms but only 19.5% of all parents (840/4314) granted permission.

Reasons for refusal included poor timing, lack of interest, the child not wanting to participate, and the topic seeming irrelevant; many parents said it was the first time they were asked for informed consent for their child.
Authors recommend formative research on the parental-consent process, better communication methods and content, and oversampling; phone interviews were offered in Arabic or English.
athar_applications: Plan recruitment yield conservatively: in a Gulf school setting expect perhaps 20-50% of approached families to consent; ATHAR's Experiment 2 target of 120-200 teens may require approaching 400-800 families.
Use a short Arabic info session or voice note for parents, and send forms with clear 'why your child' framing; pilot the consent form itself with 5 parents first.
limitations: Health-topic study (smoking) may lower consent rates versus a learning game; 2011 data.

title: Researcher facilitation service (تسهيل مهمة الباحثين) – Kuwait Ministry of Education website service listing
title_ar: تسهيل مهمة الباحثين — وزارة التربية، دولة الكويت
authors: Ministry of Education, State of Kuwait
key_findings: Kuwait's Ministry of Education lists two e-services: 'Facilitating researchers' tasks' (تسهيل مهمة الباحثين) linking to an external portal (research.moe.edu.kw), and a 'study-instrument arbitration request' (طلب تحكيم أداة دراسة).
Eligibility, documents, approving department and timelines are not stated on the page; the portal did not respond through the proxy.
athar_applications: Kuwait school access requires the MoE facilitation service and likely instrument review; details must be obtained from the ministry or a Kuwaiti university partner before planning dates.
limitations: Service listing only; no procedural content verified.

title: Personal Data Protection Law No. 24 of 2023 (Jordan) – Art. 6(A)(8)-(9): processing for scientific/historical research and statistical purposes without prior consent
publisher: Ministry of Digital Economy and Entrepreneurship (official bilingual translation)
key_findings: Art. 6(A)(8): processing is lawful without prior consent or notice if necessary for scientific or historical research purposes, provided it is not aimed at taking any decision or action regarding a particular person; (9) statistical purposes, national security or public interest.
Art. 6(B): data may not be kept after the processing purpose ends unless legislation provides otherwise.
athar_applications: Jordanian law allows research processing without consent, but ATHAR should not rely on it for minors: ethics practice (CIOMS, BERA) still requires guardian permission and assent, and Art. 5(A)(4) sets one-parent consent for those lacking capacity.
Retention clause supports a fixed deletion date in the pilot data plan.
limitations: Same law catalogued as ATH-SRC-1058; this record isolates the research exception. May be merged.

title: Review of national research ethics regulations and guidelines in Middle Eastern Arab countries
key_findings: Of 13 Middle Eastern Arab countries explored, 10 national research-ethics documents from 8 countries were found; others had none.
Most documents showed deficiencies relative to Helsinki, CIOMS and ICH-GCP, and varied widely in structure, content and reference to international guidance.
Documents focus on medical/clinical research.
athar_applications: Explains why ATHAR must layer international standards (CIOMS/BERA/ERIC) on top of national rules: national texts are uneven and medical-centred.
Justifies a single 'highest common standard' protocol for all pilot countries.
limitations: 2012 snapshot; several countries have since legislated (e.g., Egypt 2020).

title: Multinational Pediatric Critical Care Research in the Arab Gulf Region across 35 Pediatric Intensive Care Units: Ethical Approval Timelines and Lessons Learned
key_findings: Six-country Gulf retrospective study with 35 PICUs; each centre obtained independent ethical approval plus data-sharing agreements.
Median IRB approval time: private hospitals 28 days (IQR 18-55), governmental 29 days (IQR 24-146), university hospitals 52 days (IQR 30-109).
Structured coordination and collaborative planning made regional approval feasible.
athar_applications: Only empirical Gulf benchmark found for approval durations: plan 4-8 weeks per ethics committee (longer tails up to ~5 months), separate from education-authority permission.
Multi-country ATHAR pilots need one ethics approval per country/institution – not one regional approval.
limitations: Retrospective medical-records research (low risk, no minors contacted); prospective studies with minors may take longer.

title: Knowledge, Attitudes, and Practice Regarding Research Ethics Committees Among Health Care Faculty at Two Public Universities in Jordan
publisher: Journal of Empirical Research on Human Research Ethics (SAGE)
key_findings: Most surveyed health-science faculty at two major Jordanian public universities had no research-ethics training at their institutions.
Knowledge of REC roles was adequate but deficient on advisory and monitoring roles; faculty raised concerns about REC member training, conflicts of interest and bias.
athar_applications: When choosing a Jordanian academic partner, ATHAR should check the partner REC's SOPs and ask for SBS-experienced reviewers; budget for ethics training of ATHAR moderators regardless.
limitations: Health-science faculty only; self-report survey.

title: UX Research with Minors: Consent vs. Assent
key_findings: Under-18 participants need a guardian's written consent plus the child's own assent; children must be free to decline or stop at any time and researchers should look for a clear verbal yes, not a nod or silence.

Guardian form should state purpose, tasks, data use/storage/protection, compensation, voluntariness and contact; teens are typically fine without a parent in the room (check with family), younger children may have a parent nearby.
Compensation: parents paid; children receive age-appropriate rewards (gift cards for 9+), confirmed with parents; be ready to stop immediately if the child seems uncomfortable.
athar_applications: Industry-practice confirmation that product UX tests with teens use the same consent+assent pair as research; ATHAR's moderator script requires an explicit spoken 'yes' recorded in the session log.
Supports a small teen-directed thank-you (book/stationery voucher) agreed with parents.
limitations: US practice article; does not address recording rules or Arab legal ages.

title: Teenager's UX: Designing for Teens
key_findings: Based on 100 users aged 13-17 in three rounds (US, UK, Australia), usability tests, home/school field studies and interviews across 210 websites and 30 apps.

Teens feel confident but perform worse than adults owing to weaker reading skills, less developed search strategies and lower patience; they dislike dense text, quickly abandon slow or cluttered sites.
Teens respond to interactive features (quizzes, games, voting), reject content labelled 'kids' or childish visuals, prefer peer-featured content, and want control over social sharing.
Method advice: realistic tasks matched to teens' interests, think-aloud, combined field observation and interviews; watch for teens blaming the design and abandoning quickly.
athar_applications: Moderators should code abandonment and 'this is childish' remarks as primary signals in Experiment 1 (matches its tone alarm threshold).
Arabic reading load must be checked with comprehension probes; teen impatience means sessions should keep reading blocks short.
limitations: Anglophone teens and websites; not games; NN/g report not peer-reviewed.

title: Ten Tenets for Usability Testing with Minors
key_findings: Derived from 91 sessions with 79 participants aged 8-14.
Two adults are required in the room (two researchers, or one researcher plus a parent/guardian) – otherwise the session does not proceed; hands and interactions stay visible on camera.
Separate consent for audio/visual recording in addition to guardian consent and child assent; parents ideally wait elsewhere and write questions down rather than interrupting.
Sessions typically 60-90 minutes; extend for neurodivergent participants; cover transport to reduce no-shows.
athar_applications: Adopted as ATHAR's 'two-adult rule' for every in-person session; remote sessions require a guardian present in the home.
Separate recording tick-box in ATHAR's parental consent template.
limitations: US lab practice with younger children (8-14); page date not shown (images 2023).

title: Using the fun toolkit and other survey methods to gather opinions in child computer interaction
publisher: Proceedings of the 2006 Conference on Interaction Design and Children (IDC '06), ACM, pp. 81-88
key_findings: Reviews known concerns with survey methods for children's opinions and their impact on child-computer interaction studies.
Presents three studies on the efficacy of the Fun Toolkit and derives guidelines for its use and for survey methods with children.
athar_applications: Cautions against relying on a single smiley/Likert 'fun' item for 13-14 year-olds; ATHAR pairs the 1-5 pulse with behavioural measures (asks for next case, voluntary continuation) as in 03's HINT_AND_DIFFICULTY_SYSTEM §6.3.
Comparative 'which case did you like more' rankings can complement absolute ratings.
limitations: Abstract only; Fun Toolkit was developed for younger children – suitability for 13-16 Arab teens is unverified.

title: Games User Research
key_findings: Community-written handbook positioning games user research as an integral part of game development and a primary source of product intelligence.
Includes chapters on methods such as the Rapid Iterative Test and Evaluation (RITE) method (Medlock, DOI 10.1093/oso/9780198794844.003.0013) and surveys in GUR.
athar_applications: Reference handbook for ATHAR's Experiment 1 session design: iterative fixes between sessions (RITE-style) are acceptable in a product playtest but not in a pre-registered research arm.
Use its playtest/survey chapters to brief moderators before Arabic adaptation.
limitations: Book content not read beyond abstract and chapter list; no teen- or Arabic-specific guidance confirmed.

title: A mathematical model of the finding of usability problems
key_findings: Across 11 studies, detection of usability problems as a function of number of test users or evaluators is well modelled as a Poisson process.
Early test results can estimate how many problems remain and how many more sessions are needed; for a 'medium' example, ~16 evaluations were worth their cost with maximum benefit/cost at four.
athar_applications: Supports small iterative rounds (5-8 teens per round) for finding interface problems in Experiment 1 – distinct from estimating rates (solve rate, % aha), which needs larger n.
limitations: Problem-discovery logic only; discovery probability per user varies widely (see ATH-SRC-2139).

title: Beyond the five-user assumption: Benefits of increased sample sizes in usability testing
key_findings: With 60 users tested and random subsets drawn, some 5-user sets found 99% of problems while others found only 55%.
With 10 users the worst set still found 80% of problems; with 20 users, 95%.
athar_applications: Justifies ATHAR's Experiment 1 floor of ~20 teens (not 5) when stakes are a go/no-go product decision across two age bands and several dialect backgrounds.
limitations: Single-system study with adults.

title: Do procedures for verbal reporting of thinking have to be reactive? A meta-analysis and recommendations for best reporting methods
key_findings: Meta-analysis of 94 studies (~3,500 participants) comparing concurrent verbalisation with silent control: pure think-aloud effect on accuracy is indistinguishable from zero (r ≈ -.03).
Directed verbalisations (explaining, describing specific information) were predicted to and can change thought processes and performance – so instructions matter.
athar_applications: ATHAR's think-aloud instruction is 'say what you are thinking' – never 'explain why' during play; explanations are saved for the retrospective interview, to avoid altering the reasoning being measured.
Supports using think-aloud as response-process evidence in Experiment 1 (EDUCATIONAL_VALIDATION_PLAN stage 1).
limitations: Mostly adult lab tasks; reactivity in teens and in Arabic diglossic speech not studied.

title: Rethinking Thinking Aloud: A Comparison of Three Think-Aloud Protocols
publisher: Proceedings of the 2018 CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (ACM), pp. 1-12
key_findings: Compared concurrent, retrospective and hybrid think-aloud on a library website (task performance, experience, problems found, cost).

Concurrent think-aloud found more problems than retrospective, matched the hybrid, showed no reactivity, received average-to-positive ratings, and cost evaluators far less time (the other two roughly doubled testing and analysis time).
athar_applications: Default for ATHAR Experiment 1: concurrent think-aloud during play + short retrospective interview only on key moments (aha, abandonment), not full replay – cheaper and as informative.
limitations: Adult participants; website not game; language of participants not stated in abstract (first author at Umm Al-Qura University).

title: Comparing Two Methods of Usability Testing in Saudi Arabia: Concurrent Think-Aloud vs. Co-Discovery
publisher: International Journal of Human–Computer Interaction 37:118-130 (Taylor & Francis)
key_findings: Study in Saudi Arabia comparing concurrent think-aloud (single participant) with co-discovery (pairs).
Co-discovery found more minor layout/functionality problems and was rated easier, less tiring and more natural by participants; task performance did not differ.
Concurrent think-aloud was more cost-effective and equally good at revealing high-severity problems.
athar_applications: Offer co-discovery in pairs (same-gender friends) as an option for shy 13-14 year-olds in Experiment 1 – more natural talk in Arabic; keep single think-aloud as default for response-process coding.
Pair sessions change the unit of analysis – record which mode was used.
limitations: Adult Saudi participants; abstract-level reading.

title: Cultural cognition in usability evaluation
key_findings: Cultural differences affect four elements of think-aloud evaluation: instructions and tasks, users' verbalisations, the evaluator's reading of the user, and the user-evaluator relationship.
Recommends matching task presentation to users' cultural background and recognises differing effects of thinking aloud on performance and non-verbal behaviour across cultures.
athar_applications: For Arab teens, authority distance (adult moderator = teacher-like figure) may suppress criticism; ATHAR uses young moderators from the same dialect region and explicit 'you are testing us, not yourself' framing.
limitations: East Asian vs Western comparison; Arab contexts not studied.

title: What happened to remote usability testing? An empirical study of three methods
key_findings: Remote synchronous testing (real-time, moderator separated spatially) was virtually equivalent to conventional lab think-aloud in results.
Remote asynchronous methods were considerably more time-consuming for participants and identified fewer problems (per abstract).
athar_applications: Remote moderated (video-call, screen share, camera off) sessions are a valid Experiment 1 mode when school access is slow – with a guardian present at home and no video recording of the teen.
Unmoderated asynchronous tests are unsuitable for response-process evidence.
limitations: 2007 adult study; abstract truncated after asynchronous finding.

title: Sample sizes for saturation in qualitative research: A systematic review of empirical tests
key_findings: Systematic review of 23 articles testing saturation empirically or by modelling.

Empirical studies reached saturation within 9-17 interviews or 4-8 focus groups, especially with homogeneous populations and narrow objectives; multi-country or heterogeneous studies needed larger samples.
athar_applications: Experiment 1 interview component: ~9-17 teens per relatively homogeneous stratum; because ATHAR mixes 2 age bands, 2+ countries and 3 dialect groups, saturation per stratum needs more than the 20-30 total – so the qualitative claims should be per pooled theme, not per subgroup.
Experiment 3 teacher interviews (5-8 teachers) are below typical saturation – findings are exploratory.
limitations: Mostly health research; 'code saturation' differs from 'meaning saturation'.

title: The Kappa Statistic in Reliability Studies: Use, Interpretation, and Sample Size Requirements
key_findings: Explains weighted/unweighted kappa and factors influencing its magnitude: prevalence, bias and non-independent ratings.
Recommends confidence intervals and provides sample-size tables for kappa reliability studies.
athar_applications: Experiment 2's kappa ≥ 0.70 criterion between automatic observations O4/O7 and human coding should be reported with a CI and with prevalence of each code; low-prevalence codes need more sessions than the 40-60 currently planned (see playbook simulation).
limitations: Clinical-ratings context; abstract-level reading.

title: Objecting to experiments that compare two unobjectionable policies or treatments
publisher: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 116(22):10723-10728
key_findings: Across 16 studies with 5,873 participants from three populations and nine domains, people often rated A/B tests comparing two policies as inappropriate even when implementing either policy untested was seen as acceptable (the 'A/B effect').
The effect held among more educated, science-literate people and relevant professionals, and persisted even with no reason to prefer A or B.
athar_applications: Parents and schools may object to Experiment 2's randomisation even though both arms are harmless – the consent letter must explain plainly that both versions are full learning experiences and the comparison exists to choose the better one; offer the other version after the study.
Do not present randomisation as 'experimenting on children'; ATHAR's information sheet uses 'two versions of the game'.
limitations: US online samples; Arab parents not studied.

title: Editorial Expression of Concern: Experimental evidence of massive-scale emotional contagion through social networks
publisher: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 111(29):10779
key_findings: PNAS expressed concern that Facebook's 2014 News Feed experiment (Kramer et al., doi 10.1073/pnas.1320040111) may not have fully followed principles of informed consent and opt-out, although authors relied on Facebook's Data Use Policy as consent.

The notice stated Facebook, as a private company, was not obliged to follow the Common Rule when collecting data; Cornell's IRB judged the project outside its purview because Facebook ran it for internal purposes.
athar_applications: Canonical example of why the 'it's just product testing' line fails when results are published as science: ATHAR will not publish any finding from data collected under product-test terms without ethics review; claim-bearing studies are designed as research from day one.
Terms of service never substitute for parental consent and teen assent in ATHAR pilots.
limitations: Adult platform users. Notice text re-read in full on PMC (PMC4115552) on 2026-10-27. PubMed links the notice to DOI 10.1073/pnas.1412583111, which Crossref lists as a separate same-page publisher 'Correction'; the notice's own DOI per Crossref and PMC is 10.1073/pnas.1412469111 (used here). [Corrected/Clarified 2026-10-27 by deep-card review]

title: 'Voice' is not enough: conceptualising Article 12 of the United Nations Convention on the Rights of the Child
key_findings: Argues that shorthand like 'pupil voice' understates the obligation of UNCRC Article 12 to give children's views due weight.
Proposes a four-element model – Space, Voice, Audience and Influence – for implementing the right in education.
athar_applications: Design principle for ATHAR co-design: teens get a safe space and voice in sessions, an audience (named decision-maker reads their feedback) and influence (debrief letter states what changed because of them) – also an ethical 'benefit to participants' argument for committees.
limitations: Conceptual/legal analysis from Northern Ireland; not empirical about games.

title: Overall Assessment of Human Research and Ethics Committees in the United Arab Emirates
publisher: Journal of Empirical Research on Human Research Ethics 12(2):71-78 (SAGE)
key_findings: Among UAE human research ethics committees surveyed, 90% followed ICH-GCP, 66.6% had operated more than 5 years and 95% reviewed proposals within 8 weeks; 56% also reviewed scientific merit.
Fewer than 30% had systems for funding transparency or adverse-event reporting; dedicated budgets (20%) and member training (25%) were often lacking.
athar_applications: Planning assumption for UAE: ≤8 weeks for ethics review, and expect some committees to also critique scientific design – ATHAR's protocol must include the sample-size rationale.
limitations: Health-sector committees; 2017 data; abstract only.

title: Institutional Review Board (IRB) – Overview of the Committee, Deanship of Research, Jordan University of Science and Technology
authors: Jordan University of Science and Technology – Deanship of Research
publisher: Jordan University of Science and Technology (just.edu.jo)
key_findings: JUST's IRB, established in 2006 with King Abdullah University Hospital, reviews all research involving human participants, funded or unfunded, before it begins, and may approve, reject, monitor or require modifications.
Membership of at least five, including at least one unaffiliated member and one non-scientist.
athar_applications: Jordanian path: a university IRB reviews 'all research involving human participants' – ATHAR's Jordan pilot needs an academic PI at a Jordanian university (or an IRB willing to review external protocols).
limitations: Origin in clinical trials; page does not address social/educational research or minors explicitly; legal basis not stated.

title: Ethics Review Committee – College of Life Sciences, Kuwait University
authors: Kuwait University – College of Life Sciences
key_findings: The College of Life Sciences ERC acts as the college IRB, reviewing human-subjects research proposals by faculty and students.
Reviews must comply with Kuwaiti law, Ministry of Health rules and Kuwait University policies, and evaluate protocols against the Nuremberg Code, Belmont Report and Declaration of Helsinki.
athar_applications: Kuwait path: academic partner's college ERC for ethics review, then Ministry of Education facilitation (ATH-SRC-2128); confirm which KU college reviews educational/psychological studies with minors.
limitations: Scope for education research and minors not stated; application steps not visible.

title: Standing Committee for Scientific Research Ethics – King Saud University (Deanship of Scientific Research)
title_ar: اللجنة الدائمة لأخلاقيات البحث العلمي — جامعة الملك سعود
authors: King Saud University – Deanship of Scientific Research
key_findings: KSU's local research ethics committee is registered with the National Committee of Bioethics (registration R-01-H 002, dated 10/10/1428H).

The university's research-ethics system has sub-committees for research on humans, on animals, and for humanities and social research; the standing committee approves sub-committee recommendations and registers approved research.
athar_applications: Shows that Saudi university committees do review humanities/social research – an education or psychology faculty at a university with a registered committee is the practical Saudi ethics route for ATHAR pilots.
limitations: No timelines or minors-specific rules on the page.
